meta.subtitle: AI power-delivery specialist; a strong second quarter and a growing backlog, but a deep Bear case holds the call at HOLD

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Vicor a HOLD with a 12-month target range of $300 to $375 against a price of $268.34 on September 23, 2026. Vicor designs and manufactures modular power components and systems, and its Advanced Products line now sells mainly into data center and hyperscaler computing, including power delivery for AI processors. Second-quarter 2026 results were strong: revenue rose sharply year over year, backlog more than doubled from a year earlier, and operating margin sits well above its FY24 level. The financials and growth sections quantify each. The rating does not rest on doubts about the business. It comes from the shape of the outcomes. Our scenarios give a positive expected value, but the Bear case is deep: in a customer-concentrated business with an FY24 operating loss in its recent history, a stall in earnings growth would cost the stock a large part of its current-year multiple. The shares have also fallen well below their 52-week high without an explanation in any source we hold, which the valuation section weighs. On our weights, reward against that downside falls just short of the BUY line, so the derived label is HOLD, and the call is close.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Vicor Corporation designs, develops, manufactures, and markets modular power components and power systems that convert electrical power for electrically powered devices. It was incorporated in 1981 and is headquartered in Andover, Massachusetts. Management groups the portfolio into Advanced Products, which are largely used to implement its proprietary Factorized Power Architecture and sell mainly into data center and hyperscaler computing, and Brick Products, its established integrated converters for aerospace and defense, industrial, instrumentation and transportation customers. Vicor reports as a single segment, and the pack carries no dollar split of revenue between the two categories. FY25 revenue was $407.7 million, up 13.5%, with net income of $118.6 million and diluted EPS of $2.61.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Vicor is moving from many low-volume customers toward a small number of large OEM, ODM and contract-manufacturer accounts, with Advanced Products sales concentrated in data center and hyperscaler computing. The order book, the second-quarter results and the rise in royalty revenue show that shift paying off. Management also intends to raise the share of revenue it earns from licensing its intellectual property. Against that, consensus already models a steep two-year ramp, capacity in the existing fab is filling, and a few large customers can move results. The stock's value therefore turns less on whether the business is good than on how much of FY27's consensus earnings it delivers and what the market then pays for them. Our scenarios put that value above today's price on average, but with a Bear deep enough to keep the call at HOLD.

catalysts: Conversion of the larger order book into revenue; the growth section gives the backlog figures.
Progress toward a second fab for 2nd Gen VPD ChiPs, which would add capacity if demand keeps rising.
Royalty revenue holding near its second-quarter level, and progress on management's stated intent to expand licensing.
Delivery against consensus FY27 estimates, which our Base case assumes.
risks: A deep Bear case: if earnings growth stalls, the valuation section shows how far the multiple could fall.
Customer concentration: a few large customers set the pace of orders.
Royalty revenue is uneven, and it lifted both second-quarter growth and margin.
Trade policy, tariffs and export controls, detailed under systemic risks.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Second-quarter 2026 total net revenues were $143.4 million, up 26.9% sequentially from $113.0 million and up 49.3% year over year. Gross margin rose to 58.0% of revenue from 55.2% in the prior quarter, which the MD&A attributes primarily to higher sales volume, including royalty revenue, partly offset by higher freight-in and tariff spending. A year earlier the gross-margin line was 65.3%, but that quarter included a $45.0 million patent litigation settlement; the same settlement lifted the FY25 gross margin to 63.6%, so neither is a clean product-based baseline. Operating expenses rose sequentially to $48.2 million from $45.5 million, as higher selling, general and administrative expense outweighed lower research and development expense, and the second-quarter operating margin was 24.3%. Net income was $49.8 million, or $1.04 per diluted share, against $20.7 million, or $0.44, in the prior quarter and $41.2 million, or $0.91, a year earlier. Management notes that both 2026 quarters include tax benefits from excess deductions related to share-based compensation, so net income runs ahead of what operations alone produced. FY25 produced a 20.1% operating margin, a sharp recovery from FY24, when the operating margin was -0.4% and diluted EPS was $0.14. On a trailing-twelve-month basis the operating margin is 18.6% and the net margin is 30.6%; net margin sits above operating margin because of the 2026 tax benefits and other income, both inside the trailing window, and not because of the 2025 settlement, which falls outside it.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: Cash and cash equivalents were $453.6 million at June 30, 2026, up 12.2% sequentially from $404.2 million, and the condensed balance sheet in the July 21, 2026 release lists no borrowings among its liabilities. The trailing-twelve-month current ratio is 13.25. The accrued-litigation liability carried at the end of 2025 is gone from the June balance sheet, consistent with the award payment the cash-flow section describes. Inventories rose 10.2% sequentially, which the MD&A attributes to anticipated volume to fulfill backlog. Management states its belief that cash from operations together with available cash will be sufficient to fund planned operational needs and capital equipment purchases for the foreseeable future. On these figures we agree: the steps toward a second fab should not require outside capital, although the pack gives no cost for that fab.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow was $34.0 million in the second quarter, after $3.9 million used in operations in the prior quarter, which absorbed a $28.6 million payment of an award for past litigation; a year earlier, second-quarter operating cash flow was $65.2 million. Capital expenditures were $11.2 million in the second quarter, against $12.4 million in the prior quarter and $6.2 million a year earlier. FY25 free cash flow was $119.2 million, an FCF margin of 29.2%, and the company repurchased $35.2 million of stock, a modest return next to that cash generation. The trailing FCF yield is 0.4%. That low figure reflects both the valuation and weaker cash generation inside the trailing window, which includes the operating outflow after the award payment and capital spending running well above the year-ago pace.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing figures Vicor trades at 86.0x earnings, 26.1x sales and 120.1x EV/EBITDA. EV/EBITDA is the richest of the three because trailing net income, lifted by the tax benefits and other income the financials section describes, runs above operating profit. The pack labels 71.9x a next-twelve-months P/E, but it matches the price over FY26E EPS of $3.73, so we read it as today's current-year multiple; on FY27E EPS of $5.62 the shares trade at about 47.7x. A year from now FY27 will be the current year, so the like-for-like reference for a multiple on FY27E a year out is today's current-year multiple, not the forward one. The pack carries no peer multiples and no history of the stock's own multiple, so our anchors are the current-year multiple, the consensus EPS estimates and the Street. Four analysts cover the stock, all at Buy, with a consensus target of $386.25, a median of $387.50 and a range of $320.00 to $450.00. Over the past 52 weeks the shares traded between $47.56 and $382.65. At $268.34 they sit well below the high, and no source in the pack explains the fall. It cuts both ways for our scenarios. The market has already marked the stock down once without a stated cause, so our Bear needs a real stall in earnings, not a change in sentiment alone, to take the price much lower. And an unexplained drop in a customer-concentrated name may reflect information the pack does not hold, which is one reason we do not weight the Bear below the Bull.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Demand keeps the backlog growing, the second fab moves ahead, and royalty revenue holds near its second-quarter level, so investors pay for growth beyond FY27. We take the top of the Street target range, $450.00, which values FY27E EPS of $5.62 above today's 71.9x current-year multiple and below the 86.0x trailing P/E.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The backlog converts and Vicor delivers FY27E EPS of $5.62, but royalty revenue is uneven and growth beyond FY27 slows. We apply 60x to that EPS, a moderate step down from today's 71.9x current-year multiple because a year from now the multiple must be paid for growth beyond FY27, which no estimate on the page covers. That gives $337.20, inside the Street range and below the $386.25 consensus.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A large customer delays or cuts orders, or an alternative power architecture wins designs, and royalty revenue falls back, so EPS a year out, when FY27 is the current year, stays near the FY26E $3.73 instead of reaching $5.62. We apply 40x to that EPS, a cut of a little under half from today's 71.9x current-year multiple, because the growth that multiple pays for would have stopped. That gives $149.20, inside the 52-week range.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Each scenario states its anchor in its driver; this paragraph argues the Bear multiple and the weights. The Bear's 40x is the larger judgment, and we compare it with today's 71.9x current-year multiple, the like-for-like basis. A deeper cut is defensible: the stock traded far lower within the past year, and FY24's operating loss shows how fast earnings in this business can fall. A shallower cut is defensible too: in the Bear, earnings stall rather than fall, the IP, the licensing stream and the cash balance remain, and a one-year stall need not end growth beyond it. We set the Bear multiple at the middle of those arguments. We give the Bull and the Bear 25% each and the Base 50%. In the Bull's favor, the backlog more than doubled from a year earlier, the second-quarter operating margin recovered, and all four covering analysts rate the stock Buy. Against it, the Bull needs more than consensus delivery: it needs the market to pay above today's current-year multiple a year out, while existing fab capacity is getting closer to full utilization and royalty revenue that rose sharply from a year earlier has to hold up. In the Bear's favor, the risk factors say delays from a relative few large customers have already produced lower than expected revenue, FY24 ended with an operating loss, and no source explains the stock's fall from its high. Against it, the backlog consists of orders scheduled to ship within twelve months, which gives near-term visibility the Bear has to overcome. We find nothing on the page that makes either tail more likely than the other, so we weight them equally. The probability-weighted value is $318.40, an expected upside of +18.7%, against a bear-case downside of -44.4%, for reward/risk of 0.42x. Expected upside clears the 10.0% BUY bar, but reward/risk falls short of 0.50x, so HOLD is the derived label. The call is close and rests on two judgments, the Bear multiple and the even split of the tails. Tested toward the Bull side, a Bear at 45x, five points of weight moved from Bear to Bull, or a Base that holds today's current-year multiple on FY27E would each derive BUY. Tested toward the Bear side, a Bear at 35x or five points moved from Bull to Bear leaves HOLD with a lower expected upside. We think that Bear multiple and equal tails are the honest reading of this page, but a reader who gives the backlog more weight than the concentration risk would reach BUY.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Vicor reports as a single reportable segment, shown here as one consolidated total. Management runs two product categories within it. Advanced Products serve large OEMs, ODMs and their contract manufacturers, with sales currently concentrated in data center and hyperscaler computing, where they deliver power on server motherboards, in server racks and across datacenter infrastructure; the growth section covers their second-quarter rise. Brick Products serve a fragmented base in aerospace and defense electronics, industrial equipment, instrumentation and test equipment, and transportation; their net revenues grew 2.4% sequentially in the second quarter, which the MD&A attributes primarily to improved market demand. Export sales were approximately 46.0% of second-quarter net revenues, against 48.9% in the prior quarter. The strategy deliberately trades a broad, diversified customer base for fewer, larger customers.

moatFactors.name: Proprietary power-conversion IP
moatFactors.body: According to the MD&A, many of Vicor's products incorporate patented or proprietary high-frequency switching topologies, often implemented in proprietary semiconductor circuitry, materials and packaging. The clearest evidence that this IP has value beyond Vicor's own products is royalty revenue from licensing it to third parties, a share of revenue management intends to expand. The pack does not say who the licensees are or how long the agreements run.

moatFactors.name: AI power-delivery position
moatFactors.body: In the MD&A of its June-quarter 10-Q, Vicor says it has established a leadership position in powering high-performance processors used for AI, with customers among leading processor and accelerator designers. In his July 21, 2026 comment, the CEO said that with its 2nd Gen VPD IP, Vicor is 'uniquely equipped' to overcome the power system challenges facing future TPUs, GPUs and Wafer Scale Engines. Both are the company's own claims; the pack carries no independent data on share in this market, so we rate the factor on the backlog and Advanced Products growth rather than on those statements.

moatFactors.name: Manufacturing integration
moatFactors.body: Vicor builds advanced parts in its own ChiP fab and, per the MD&A, has moved some outsourced manufacturing steps in-house to limit supply-chain disruption. That control supports differentiation, but it ties margins to factory utilization, and some Advanced Products still rely on outsourced package process steps.

businessMoat.durability: The advantage is real but bounded. The IP, the licensing stream and the investment in a second fab point to an edge that can last several years. The limits are scale, cyclicality and the customer concentration the risks section details, plus the company's own risk factors on competitors' product introductions and price reductions. On competing architectures, the pack's single source is the CEO's July 21, 2026 comment, which argues that the industry's move to point-of-load regulators 'merely trades off one handicap' for another, and that feeding IVRs with a current multiplier 'is an incremental opportunity for Vicor.' That is the company's view. Our own risk view is that alternative power architectures could compete for the same designs, but the pack carries no evidence on competitors' share or pricing, so we do not describe competition as intensifying. On balance the moat is narrow: strong enough to support high margins in good periods, not wide enough to insulate the company from the electronics cycle or from a large customer's decision.

points: Advanced Products drove the second quarter. Their net revenues rose 45.0% sequentially, which the MD&A attributes primarily to improved market demand and higher royalty revenue. The press-release income statement shows royalty revenue of $30,426 thousand in the second quarter of 2026 against $10,353 thousand a year earlier. Backlog, defined as orders scheduled to ship within the next 12 months, reached $380 million, up 26% sequentially and 145% from $155 million a year earlier. The test is whether that backlog ships on schedule.

Licensing is a separate stream. The MD&A states an intent to expand the percentage of revenue from licensing intellectual property to third parties. In the press-release income statement, royalty revenue has no cost line of its own, since cost is reported for product revenues only, so higher royalties add to gross margin without a matching cost. The risk is that royalties depend on negotiated agreements and need not recur at the second quarter's level.

Capacity could become a constraint if demand keeps rising. On July 21, 2026, the CEO said rising demand 'is absorbing increased capacity within our first ChiP fab' and that, as the company gets closer to full capacity utilization, it is taking steps toward a second fab for high current density 2nd Gen VPD ChiPs. No source says shipments are limited by capacity today. What matters is the timing and cost of the second fab, neither of which the pack gives.

Consensus models a steep ramp, with FY26E revenue of about $622.3 million, up 53%, and FY27E revenue of $945.4 million. Those estimates need both continued AI and datacenter demand and the capacity to serve it, and our Base case assumes they are met.

The second-quarter gross margin quoted in the financials section sits above the trailing-twelve-month 56.6%, but that run-rate leans partly on royalty revenue and carries the royalty caveat above. The FY25 margin is not a baseline either, since it included the settlement the financials section describes.

management.leadership: The April 30, 2026 proxy names Dr. Vinciarelli as President and Chief Executive Officer and Mr. Schmidt as Chief Financial Officer; the July 21, 2026 release gives their full names as Dr. Patrizio Vinciarelli and James F. Schmidt. For 2025 the named executive officers were those two and three Corporate Vice Presidents. The proxy describes a centralized process: Dr. Vinciarelli, with input from the Corporate Vice President of Human Resources, makes periodic compensation recommendations to the Compensation Committee for the other executives. The pack gives no tenures for these officers.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation favors reinvestment. Vicor pays no dividend, and capital spending has stepped up as it adds manufacturing capacity, with the second fab the next decision; the balance-sheet section explains why that should not need outside capital. Buybacks are Vicor's sole cash return, and the cash-flow section weighs their size. The diluted share count was 47,708 thousand in the second quarter of 2026 against 45,077 thousand a year earlier, so per-share results have absorbed dilution despite the repurchases; the proxy names stock options as the main equity award. The open question is the return on new capacity, which depends on sustained orders from the few large customers the risks section discusses.
management.governance: Governance rests on the proxy statement filed April 30, 2026. Vicor holds say-on-pay votes every three years. The 2023 vote approved executive pay on an advisory basis, and the 2026 proxy put a new say-on-pay vote to the 2026 Annual Meeting, whose result is not in the pack. Pay combines base salary, sales-incentive cash bonuses for certain sales and marketing staff, stock options and an employee stock purchase plan; executives are employees at will without employment contracts. One related-party arrangement stands out. Director and nominee Andrew T. D'Amico also serves as general counsel for intellectual-property matters for a fee of approximately $35,974 per month, subject to annual adjustment, plus an incentive fee of 3% of royalties under certain license agreements he negotiates. Those incentive fees are limited to $1,000,000 in aggregate, although that amount may be increased by mutual agreement, including when he negotiates additional license agreements. In 2025 his license-based incentive fees were $21,596 of the $2,073,076 he received in compensation and reimbursement, most of which was income from option exercises. The incentive is small today, but because it can grow with the licensing the company plans to expand, and because the general counsel sits on the board, it merits continued attention.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt in the pack does not include the beneficial-ownership table, so we cannot quantify insider or institutional holdings. The arrangement with Mr. D'Amico described under governance is the one insider economic interest the excerpt discloses.

idiosyncratic: Customer concentration: the 10-K filed March 2, 2026 says the focus on high-volume OEM, ODM and contract-manufacturer customers has caused the actions of a relative few to disproportionately influence results, and that unanticipated delays from certain large customers have resulted in lower than expected revenue. The MD&A adds that these customers' forecasts are subject to scheduling changes on short notice. This is the main path to our Bear case, and the pack does not name the customers or their shares of revenue.
Valuation: at the multiples the valuation section sets out, a slowdown in growth would cut the multiple as well as earnings, which is why the Bear case is deep.

Cyclicality and margin volatility: as recently as FY24 the company posted an operating loss, and the MD&A says quarterly gross margin may vary with production volumes, licensing income, average selling prices, unit costs, product mix and tariffed raw materials.

Royalty dependence and comparability: royalty revenue lifted both second-quarter growth and margin, subject to the recurrence caveat in the growth section, and the 2025 settlement distorts year-over-year comparisons, as the financials section details.

Supply chain: some Advanced Products depend on outsourced package process steps. The MD&A says supply-chain disruptions have in the past negatively impacted operating results, and that the steps taken to mitigate them, such as moving outsourced steps in-house and expediting deliveries at a cost premium, have at times reduced revenue, gross margin, operating profit and cash flow.
risks.systemic: Trade policy is the main external exposure. Per the 10-K filed March 2, 2026, sales outside the United States were 50.8% of 2025 net revenues, and China and Hong Kong accounted for approximately 11.9%. Section 301 tariff costs rose 76.1% in 2025 to about 1.8% of net revenues, reducing gross margin, and the company cannot estimate further duty-drawback recoveries. Export controls and a stronger U.S. dollar may also reduce end-demand. Beyond trade, growth is tied to AI and datacenter capital spending, so a slowdown in that investment cycle would reach orders directly, and the electronics supply chain is cyclical. Pressure on U.S. defense budgets would weigh on the aerospace and defense demand that supports Brick Products.

body: We rate Vicor HOLD with a target range of $300 to $375. The business is performing: the order book, the second-quarter results and royalty growth support our Base case. The rating comes from the scenarios. They give an expected upside of +18.7%, but against a Bear that would take the shares far lower, reward/risk is 0.42x, below the 0.50x a BUY needs. As the valuation section shows, the call is close, and modest changes toward the Bull side derive BUY.

We would move to BUY if the next quarters show the backlog still growing and royalty revenue holding near its second-quarter level, which would argue for a shallower Bear, or if the share price fell a few percent with the scenarios unchanged, since the page's own math derives BUY just below today's price. We would move toward SELL if a large customer's orders slip enough to shrink the backlog, or if the price rose to about our Base value of $337.20 with no change in the scenarios, where the page's math would derive SELL.
